reason:
This is the soundest citation in the batch and I could not break it. I tried three ways: the wording, the line number, and the volume.

THE WORDING. I downloaded the Project Gutenberg text the evidence names, ebook 8601, The Early Poems of Alfred Lord Tennyson, this run. The poem's last line reads ‘To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.’ Exact, comma for comma, and the card's full stop is the poem's. It matters that the surrounding lines in that text carry Tennyson's apostrophised forms, ‘Tho’ much is taken, much abides; and tho’’ and ‘Match'd with an aged wife’, and the quoted line has none of them to get wrong. There is nothing in it that could have drifted.

THE LINE NUMBER. I did not take 70 on trust. I counted the verse lines of the poem in that text, from ‘It little profits that an idle king,’ to ‘To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.’, ignoring blank lines: 70 exactly. The locator is right and the line is the closing line.

THE VOLUME AND THE DATE. The 1842 Poems came out in two volumes, the first largely revisions of the 1830 and 1832 pieces and the second the new work, and Ulysses is in the second with Morte d'Arthur, Locksley Hall and Break, break, break. The editorial headnote in the Gutenberg volume states it directly and adds the fact that closes off the usual drift risk with Tennyson, who revised all his life: ‘First published in 1842, no alterations were made in it subsequently.’ So the 1842 wording is also the wording of every later text, and citing the Moxon volume cannot put the card at odds with a reader's modern edition. The byline is right for that imprint too: the title page reads Poems by Alfred Tennyson, and he is not Lord Tennyson until 1884, so ‘Alfred Tennyson’ is correct and matches the form the ledger already holds.

THE GATES. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], alfred tennyson at 1 of 3, months [1], not banned, so he is free. I checked what that January line is, because two cards from one poem would be a real objection: it is ‘Ring out the old, ring in the new’ from In Memoriam section CIV, a different work entirely, so there is no collision. Scope: verse, 1842, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Nothing on the misattribution list touches it. Publishable: it is the line of a man past his strength deciding to go on, with no wound and nothing to warn about. Tag Poetry is right; this is a dramatic monologue, which is a poem and not a play, so Drama would have been the wrong bucket. The source line is 88 characters, leads with the name, carries no em dash and no straight quote. Theme fit is as close to the month's own sentence as the year is likely to get: ‘Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will’ is Courage in Trial, and the card carries the resolve without the weakness, which is what six in the morning wants.

WHY I HAVE PUT SOMETHING IN betterCitation ANYWAY, WITHOUT REFUTING. The speaker parenthesis is in the wrong place. Rule 5 puts the speaker in parentheses after the locator, and the file's practice is speaker first, imprint or translation last: ‘(Santiago) (Scribner, 1952)’, ‘(Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)’, ‘(Philosophy) (trans. H. R. James, 1897)’. The card as proposed reads ‘... the closing line, Poems, vol. 2 (Edward Moxon, 1842) (Ulysses)’, which trails the speaker after the imprint and, worse, sets a bare ‘(Ulysses)’ at the end of a line that already begins ‘Alfred Tennyson, Ulysses’, so the name reads as a stutter rather than as a speaker. The version in betterCitation puts the line number in the locator where it is useful, names Ulysses as the speaker immediately after it, and closes with the imprint, at 97 characters. That is a formatting fix, not a correction: the citation itself is sound either way, and nothing false reaches the card as proposed. Ships.
